dawn song, starts with and has more after 0:16 and 0:24, 0:56, 1:02, 1:07, 1:39 palmeri Curve-billed Thrashers (plus single first, short notes after 0:34 etc.) among much mimetic material, other species including Western Tanager, Acorn Woodpecker, and perhaps Gila Woodpecker; it is moving regularly among the 2m mesquites in which it is singing just outside the riparian zone; adult male; interval shortened at 0:12 and 0:45, recording getting worse in terms of rooster, House Finch, etc.; audible wingbeats by the adult male as it moved a short ways after 1:20 (good);

Marcus Breemer tekent hierbij aan: "Ik ben er wel van overtuigd dat het een brilduiker is. De vorm van de elementen komt mooi overeen met andere opnames (bv. https://xeno-canto.org/765958). De grondtoon van een brilduiker varieert tussen 1.5 en 2 kHz met 1e harmonische tussen 3-4 kHz (beide afhankelijk van Dopplereffect denk ik), dat is bij jou ook. Maar wat er misschien nog meer op wijst is dat de frequentie van vleugelslagen precies hetzelfde is, nl. 9 Hz. Ik heb daarvoor het interval van 17.00 tot 20.00 sec genomen, waarin 27 vleugelslagen zitten; bij jouw eerdere brilduiker was dat ook zo, 27 slagen in 3 sec = 9 Hz (https://xeno-canto.org/652209), bij https://xeno-canto.org/765958 ook 27/3 sec=9 Hz en bij mijn brilduikeropname ook 9 Hz."

Marcus Breemer notes: "I am convinced that it is a Goldeneye. The shape of the elements corresponds nicely with other recordings (e.g. https://xeno-canto.org/765958). The keynote of a Goldeneye varies between 1.5 and 2 kHz with the 1st harmonic between 3-4 kHz (both depending on the Doppler effect, I think), that applies to you too. But what might even indicate that the frequency of wing beats is exactly the same, namely: 9 Hz. I used the interval from 17:00 to 20:00 sec, which contains 27 wing beats; this was also the case with your previous spectacled diver, 27 beats in 3 sec = 9 Hz (https://xeno-canto.org/652209) , at https://xeno-canto.org/765958 also 27/3 sec=9 Hz and at my spectacled recording also 9 Hz."
